content: The integration of evidence-based policies for managing critically ill infants and children into national healthcare programs requires a well-structured and participatory approach. This process involves adapting and implementing these policies, which may include revising or preparing national guidelines and protocols. Each country is expected to tailor these recommendations to align with their unique social, cultural, and economic contexts. To achieve this, countries are encouraged to engage in discussions with key stakeholders to decide on the adoption and integration of these recommendations into their national healthcare systems. Creating an environment conducive to the use of these recommendations is essential. This includes promoting behavior change among healthcare practitioners to adopt evidence-based practices. Local professional societies can play a significant role in this process, and an inclusive, participatory approach should be encouraged. The World Health Organization (WHO) has extensive experience in introducing its guidelines and tools into national programs. The medications recommended in this document are included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (2015). The model list serves as a guide for developing national and institutional lists of essential medicines. The WHO's 2014 report on global antimicrobial resistance highlights the growing global challenge of antibiotic resistance. This issue is critical when reviewing national drug lists and policies, and countries should strengthen their plans to address antimicrobial resistance. Monitoring and evaluation should be integral to the implementation of these guidelines to derive lessons for future use and further implementation. Priority should be given to assessing the impact of strong recommendations on the quality of care. National child health programs should use this guideline to collect and report data on the management of sick infants and children. Key areas for monitoring include: The prevalence of critically ill infants and children presenting at first-level health facilities. Outcomes of management. Risks of side effects, particularly from anticonvulsive treatments. The emergence of new anticonvulsants with potentially better safety profiles. Service delivery metrics, such as coverage, quality of care, and adherence to treatment protocols. Support systems, including supplies, logistics, and supervision. The WHO’s Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA) will monitor the implementation of the guideline using indicators such as the number of requests from countries for assistance in using the guideline and the number of countries applying the guideline. Additionally, MCA will track the number of downloads of the guideline document from WHO and partner websites, as well as the distribution of hard copies. Future research implications include addressing clinical research questions identified during the development of recommendations and conducting implementation research. Policy adoption and creating an enabling environment for implementation will require dialogue with policymakers and national stakeholders. Program managers will need technical support from experts experienced in delivering these interventions to prepare and implement operational plans and programs. Small-scale demonstration projects may assist in designing and scaling up training and implementation at the country level. Plans for updating the guideline include a review of the literature and updating recommendations as needed by 2019. In the interim, the steering committee will continue to identify new studies, interim research results, and reports of adverse events. If urgent changes to the recommendations are required before 2019, a guideline development group will be convened.
